topic.label: Protocol
topic.desc: Protocols and interfaces between agents, tools and services: MCP servers and clients, agent-to-agent protocols, API design, schemas and contracts, authentication flows, transports, versioning and conformance testing. Extends the base Protocol topic, which held I/O Contract and Protocol.

concepts: Building and consuming Model Context Protocol servers: tools, resources, prompts, capability negotiation and client configuration.
How agents find and call each other: agent cards, task lifecycles, messages, artifacts and handoff between agents.
Designing HTTP and RPC interfaces: resources, verbs, errors, pagination, idempotency and OpenAPI descriptions.
Describing data exactly: JSON Schema, typed contracts, validation at the boundary and clear error messages.
Who may call what: API keys, OAuth flows, scopes, token storage and consent screens, without putting secrets in code.
Moving messages: stdio, HTTP, server-sent events, WebSockets, streaming responses, timeouts and retries.
Changing an interface without breaking its users: semantic versions, deprecation, feature flags and migration guides.
Proving an implementation follows the protocol: contract tests, mock servers, fuzzing of messages and test reports.
skills: Designs the tools, inputs and outputs of an MCP server for a service and writes the server skeleton with descriptions the model can use.
Configures a client to connect to chosen servers, lists the tools it will expose and the permission each one needs.
Writes tool names and descriptions so a model picks the right tool, and tests them with sample requests; adds annotations such as read-only hints.
Writes an agent card that states skills, endpoint, input and output types and authentication so other agents can find and call it.
Defines task states, updates and cancellation between agents and what each side must do on failure or timeout.
Specifies what context, files and authority pass from one agent to another and what stays behind.
Models resources and relations as endpoints, with names, verbs and status codes chosen to match common practice.
Writes an OpenAPI description from an API, with examples and error shapes, and validates it with a linter.
Designs error bodies, pagination, rate-limit signals and idempotency keys so clients can retry safely.
Writes a JSON Schema for a message, with required fields and formats, and tests it against valid and invalid samples.
Places validation where data enters the system and makes each failure return a message that says which field is wrong and why.
Compares two versions of a schema and lists breaking changes, such as removed fields and narrowed types, that would break existing producers or consumers.
Chooses the OAuth flow for a client, lists scopes and redirect handling and says where tokens are stored.
Reviews requested scopes against what the feature uses and proposes the smallest set that still works.
Checks that keys and tokens come from the environment or a secret store, never from code or logs, and lists leaks found.
Chooses between stdio, HTTP, server-sent events and WebSockets for a use and states what each costs in complexity.
Designs how partial results stream, how a client resumes after a drop and how backpressure is handled.
Sets timeouts, retry rules with backoff and limits and shows which calls are safe to repeat.
Decides whether a change is a major, minor or patch release from the interface diff and explains the call.
Writes a deprecation notice with the sunset date, replacement and a migration path, and finds callers still using the old form.
Writes step by step migration instructions and a changelog between two versions with before and after examples.
Writes tests that check an implementation against the written contract, with one test per rule.
Builds a mock server from a schema that returns valid and error responses so clients can be tested offline.
Sends malformed and boundary-case messages to an endpoint and reports crashes, hangs and unsafe behaviour.
